michigan.apis.1514.s: Receipt for money payment made by the chief of police of the division of Thallos to the chief clerk (primicerius) of the stenographers (exceptores)

michigan.apis.1515.s: This short text summarizes declarations made, probably in 298 or 299, by Herakles and Alexander, sons of Horion, for the census conducted in the Arsinoite nome. The present text lists their holdings in the village of Karanis and its horodeiktia. It is a summary which combines the information provided by two declarations, one for the village, one for the horodeiktia (cf. nos. 4 and 5).
michigan.apis.1515.luogo: Karanis, Herakleidou meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt (?)

michigan.apis.1516.s: In this text C. Valerius Marcus declares 20 2/3 arouras of catoechic land, including a 1/4 aroura of an epibole, in the area surrounding the village of Bacchias in the Arsinoite nome.
michigan.apis.1516.luogo: Bacchias, Herakleidou meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.1520.s: Deposit of six thousand silver drachmas of imperial coinage.

michigan.apis.1521.s: The text preserves almost complete three receipts issued by a collector of asemon, i. e. silver bullion, for payments made in talents in the months of September, October, and November. In the second receipt the payment also cover a payment for lentils.

michigan.apis.1522.s: A certain Chairas acknowledges that he has surrendered or restored to Nilos certain properties, a part of which he specifically calls his own.
michigan.apis.1522.luogo: Kerkesoucha, Herakleidou meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.1524.luogo: probably Arsinoiton polis, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.1526.s: Order for the payment of pitch

michigan.apis.1527.s: Application addressed by Areios and Maron to unknown lessors, by which they request the right to sublease a date crop from them

michigan.apis.1528.s: The account contained in this text registers the receipt of payments both in money and in kind made by the grammateus Lucius to the anonymous writer. The payments are spread over the greater part of a year, but the nature of the service rendered is not specified. A word crucial in this connection has been virtually obliterated on the papyrus (line 4).
michigan.apis.1528.luogo: Oxyrhynchite nome, Middle Egypt, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.1529.s: This fragment contains the ends of Homer, liad 18.251-275. There are no variant readings.

michigan.apis.1530.s: The text is in main an account of barley distributed for the sowing of the 20th year. The dates of issue run from Hathyr 30 (= Nov. 27) to Tybi 5 (=Jan. 1). One entry departs from the pattern indicated above. At some time near or after the middle of December, 1/2 art. of barley was devoted to the preparation of malt. This is stated in l. 9 as eis bynin.

michigan.apis.1531.s: List of centurions and decurions of two auxiliary units (an unknown ala and the Cohors III Ituraeorum), giving for each the date of his enlistment in the army and of his appointment to his current grade; the names are probably given in the order of their seniority within their unit and rank. The text must come from a bureau above the level of a single military unit;On the verso, slight remnants of an (unrelated?) account, in Greek

michigan.apis.1532.s: This papyrus contains two receipts, each acknowledging payments of 20 dr. for poll tax, with 10 ob. as the extra charge, from Ptolemaios, son of Pappos, and his son Melanas. The first receipt (1-8) is for the account of the 23rd year of Commodus; the second (9-13) for the account of the 24th yr.

michigan.apis.1533.s: Papontos, son of Alypos, reports the death of his father to the secretary of the city of Oxyrhynchus
michigan.apis.1533.luogo: Oxyrhynchus, Oxyrhynchite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.1534.s: this papyrus lists a number of different herbs and spices.

michigan.apis.1535.s: Receipt for the payment of the merismos
michigan.apis.1535.luogo: probably Kerkesoucha Orous, Herakleides meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.1536.s: Contract by which Aurelius Kaetis, son of Neilos, acknowledges to have borrowed from Aurelius Hieron 152 drachmai, interest free, for one year
michigan.apis.1536.luogo: probably Theadelphia, Themistou meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.1537.s: If the text is the whole document, it cannot have included the imperial constitutio, which is said to have been prefixed (4-5) nor the copy of the will, which is said to have been appended; no doubt this is to be explained by the fact that we have is explicity described as a copy. The text consists of a petition to Vettius Gallianus, acting-epistrategos (of the Thebaid), from a certain Aurelius Apollonius also called Sarapion, an Alexandrian citizen and landholder in Diospolis Parva. It thus enhanced value since it comes from an unusual provenance. In his petition the writer complains that Osaeus, whom he describes as his father's wife and who must therefore have been his step-mother, has cheated him in respect to the property left in his father's will. A copy of the subscriptio follows, dated to a year 25. The emperor is referred to in col. ii can only be Caracalla.
k: Diospolis Par va, Thebaid, Province of Egypt

michigan.apis.1538.s: Receipt issued to John (son of) Proou for the payment of poll tax (laographia). This papyrus, along with P. Mich. inv. 1842, is unusual in that it combines Coptic and Greek. The text begins with the name of the tax and the identification of the taxpayer in Coptic. Then follows in Greek the indiction year for which the tax is payed (the year preceding the date). The amount of the tax is then recorded in Coptic, with the resumȨ and date following in Greek. Another unusual, though not unparalleled, feature is the fact that this receipt lacks a verb denoting the actual payment or reception of the tax.

michigan.apis.1539.s: Receipt issued to Kosmas (son of) John for the payment of poll tax (laographia). This papyrus, along with P. Mich. inv. 1840, is unusual in that it combines Coptic and Greek. The text begins with the name of the tax and the identification of the taxpayer in Coptic. Then follows in Greek the indiction year for which the tax is payed (the year preceding the date). The amount of the tax is then recorded in Coptic, with the resumȨ and date following in Greek. Another unusual, though not unparalleled, feature is the fact that this receipt lacks a verb denoting the actual payment or reception of the tax.

michigan.apis.1540.s: Statement of sale of some land, confirmed with an imperial oath, and directed to the strategos
k: Themistou meris, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nom; Moeris (amphodon of Arsinoiton polis)

michigan.apis.1541.s: Private letter from a pregnant woman to her mother

michigan.apis.1543.s: Letter from Sempronius to his son Gaius

michigan.apis.1544.s: Letter sent by Sempronius to his mother Satornila, filled with concerns about her welfare and about some unknown family matters

michigan.apis.1545.s: Memorandum for transport and delivery of several diversified commodities to a certain Sarapamon; the items which were delivered or made ready for transportation are noted by a dash drawn through the first word

michigan.apis.1547.s: This papyrus contains the latter part of an acknowledgement of a sale of two and a half arouras of land for the price of 370 drachmas by two brothers, Aurelius Aion and Aurelius Pharitas. The contract ends with the usual guarantees, including the guarantee of the prior right of payment to the fiscus. The signature, written by a scribe for the illiterate brothers, includes the stipulation that the past taxes in grain and money remain the responsibility of the sellers, with no time limit specified.

michigan.apis.1548.s: This papyrus contains the account of a business establishment of diversified interests. In addition to amounts paid out for wages and foodstuffs, there are frequent references to the production of cloth and clothings. Hence it is likely that these accounts belong to one of the small textile establishments in Oxyrhynchos frequently referred to in the papyri of the Roman and Byzantine periods.
michigan.apis.1548.luogo: Oxyrhynchos, Oxyrhynchite nome, Middle Egypt, province of Egypt (?)

michigan.apis.1551.s: List of cavalry(?) soldiers, with their year of enlistment and the number of years they have spent in service (stipendia). In the left margin, notes give their assignment to places or special duties

michigan.apis.1559.s: List of payments made by various persons

michigan.apis.1562.s: Notification given by Soeris, daughter of Asklepiades, to the secretaries of Oxyrhynchus that her son, Apollonios, son of Theon, has left his home city for some time
michigan.apis.1562.luogo: Oxyrhynchus, Oxyrhynchite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.1563.s: A report of chaff and hay delivered by Seuthes and isidoros, chaff collectors of Karanis in 310/311. The opening statement of the present report has been lost, and with it the name and title of the oficial to whom it was addressed. A reasonable guess is that it was addressed to the praepositus of the ffth pagus who was active in that office when Seutheus and Isidoros served as chaff collectors, i.e. in 310/311. The text that remains falls into three parts. Lines 1-25 contain a series of receipts issued by Gerontios, receiver of chaff, between Dec. 3 and 21, 311. These are duplicates, with minor verbal differences, of the receipts in no 13, 28-53, where the full name of the receiver is given as Aurelius Gerontius, son of demetrius. We learn also from no 13, 26 that he was stationed at Akanthon, not far from the harbor of Kerke. The quantities of chaff mentioned in both sets of receipts agree exactly, as do the totals receorded in No 13, 54 and line 25 of the present report. Lines 26-35 have copies of two receipts given to Setheus and isidoros by Ammonios and Heron, receivers of chaff at Arsinoe. They acknowledge delivery of 2700 lbr on Pachon 30 and 1950 lbs. in Payni, amking a total of 4650 lbs. Lines 36-42 contain two receipts for hay issued by collectors whose names are mutilated. they acknowledge receipt of 1200 lbs in all. These deliveries of chaff and hay reach a total of 5850 lbs, and added to the 45.7000 lbs covered in the receipts attributed to gerontios, they yield the grand total of 51.550 lbs. recorded in l. 44. the amount of chaff remaining to be collecetd is entered in l. 45 as 53.050 lbs. Together, the quantity delivered and the quantity outstanding equal the total levy of 104.600 lbs reported in no 13, 21. It is interesting to note that for a part of the levy, although a relatively small part, hay was accepted in place of chaff.;None of the receipts supplied by lines 26-42 is repeated in the later report submitted by Setheus and isidoros to the auditor of the Heptanomia on July 31, 314 (no 13). All deliveries apart from those made to Gerontios are there comprehended in the summary statement of line 56 that the remaining quantity -58.900 lbs- was "brought in subsequenly". Between Feb. 19 and July 314, the chaff collectors of 310/311 discgarged their liturgical obligations in full by delivering 53050 lbs to receivers.;Lines 46-50 give the date by the consuls of 314 and the subscription of the collectors written for them by a hypographeus. This feature of the document indicates that it was a report secially prepared, like no 13., for the scrutiny of some higher official, probably as we have said above the praepositus of the fifth papus.
michigan.apis.1563.luogo: Karanis, Herakleidou division, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt
k: Karanis, Herakleidou division, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.1564.s: A list of arrears due on the chaff levy of the 19th year of Galerius, i.e. 310/311. The collectors are not named, but they are idenified as Seuthes, son of Heras and Isidoros, son of ptolemaios. The list also fails to give the date on which was compliled. ;From the details provided in the list we may conclude that a large majority of the landholders at Karanis in 314 had still not discharhed their responsibility for the chaff tax due in 310/311. ;The document consists of six columns and the total quantity of chaff entered in each column was appended at the bottom of the column. The total for col. I is almost completely preserved. Very littele remains of the total for col. II and those for cols III and IV have been lost. Of the total for col. V, only oblique strokes such as mark a fraction are now visible. The total placed at the bottom of col. VI is exceptional in being perfectly preserved, but the addition is false.
michigan.apis.1564.luogo: Karanis, Herakleidou division, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.1578.s: A bid for the purchase of confiscated property. The bid is from Ptolemais, daughter of Agenor and granddaughter of Philiscos, submitted to Aelius Aphrodisios, strategus of the Oxyrhynchite nome, in the name of her daughter, Claudia Areia, for 16 arouras of catoecic land put up for sale near the epoikion of Artapatou in the middle toparchy. Ptolemais offered 3200 drachmas for 16 arouras, or 200 drachmas the aroura, a price which suggests that the land was still productive. Ptolemais and her daughter Claudia Areia, whom she mentions three times by name, owned all the land adjacent to the property upon which she was bidding. The right of neighbours to buy perhaps added weight to the bid, even when the land was in the hands of the fiscus. Neither Ptolemais nor Claudia Areia can confidently be identified in the papyri published up to now, but the husband and father was presumably a Klaudius Areius. He may have belonged to the family of Tiberius Claudius Areios who had served as strategus of the Heracleides division of the Arsinoite nome two generations earlier, 98-101
k: Artapatou, epoikion, Middle toparchy, Oxyrhynchite nome, province of Egypt;;Seimias, kleros, Middle toparchy (?), Oxyrhynchite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.1579.s: This text contains a letter from Dionysios to Theon concerning farm matters. Theon is urged by Dionysios to see to it that the cattle of Fabius remain where they are until the 12th of Tybi so that they may begin their pasture-feeding on the 13th. Dionysios points out that this woould be in keeping with Theon's own idea that the vegetable seed that had been sown should be irrigated before the pastures. The addressee is also asked to bring six bundles of charlock.

michigan.apis.1590.s: This text contains the end of a private contract (cheirographon) which refers to a delivery to be made. This could be either a transportation or a sale, for which the price has been payed in advance. Of the agreement (omologia) only the final phrases remain, followed by the "validity clause" and the stipulatory clause in Greek (in plural), to which the Latin clause is joined, in the 3rd person sg. The absence of the signature is striking, and so is the absence of the date at the end of the document. The date, however, could have been placed at the beginning of the document in accordance with scribal practice.

The whole document was presumably part of a petition. Only the latter part of the loan has survived. A loan is made by Gaius Valerius Severus to Markus Julius Casianus on the collateral of a house and grinding machine belonging to Julius Casianus in the village of Philadelphia. The amount of the loan and the rate of interest are lost, but the specifications of duties, rights, and guarantees are preserved.

michigan.apis.1661.s: This text contains the will of a testator, whose name is lost. After making specific bequests (lines 1-4), bequeaths the balance of his estate in two equal shares to his daughter Tsensarapion and to "those around" Hermias (lines 4-8). He makes a substitutio vulgaris, in case the latter do not survive him, of their children (line 8). He also notes that he has previously conveyed by deed a vineyard in the allotment of Kallikrates near the village of Teis to an unnamed party (lines 8-9).

michigan.apis.1737.s: On the one side it contains a table of the simplest of fractions (1/2) and an equally simple multiplication table (2). On the other side an iambic often found on schooltablets is written.;The outer side of the tablet, which originally was the back cover of a book of tablets, is;used for the mathematical tables, which are written along the width of the tablet. This side;was coated with a white layer that has partly come off. Because of that the text is sometimes;barely legible. Four simple vertical lines are used to divide the five columns of text. Another;such line follows the fifth column. Within the text horizontal lines are used to divide certain;portions of text. This is the case between column I 2 and 3, column III 8 and 9, column III;10 and 11 and between the items in the multiplication table at the end of column III. There is;also a vertical line separating the juxtaposed items there.;The inner side of the tablet is used for the maxim, which is written perpendicularly to the;text on the outer side. The coating on this side of the tablet is very well preserved. In this;coating a rectangle was ruled about 1 cm from the lower and right edges of the tablet and;about 1.5 cm from the upper and left edges. This seems to imitate the raised frame of a waxed;tablet. In addition, 20 horizontal lines were ruled in the coating. The first line starts 6 cm be-low;the upper line of the rectangular frame. This leaves a field of 14 x 6 cm into which the;maxim was written. The tail of the rho of "grammata" is written over the first line.

michigan.apis.1849.s: The text consists of a list of clothing and household goods, occupying all of the recto and almost two-thirds of the verso. That it formed part of the records of a pawnshop may be deduced from the occurrence of the words enechyreimai: "I have received as pledge . . ." There is no valuation of the individual items and no mention of interest. The only sum of money mentioned is at the bottom of the recto, and the amount, 20 or 30 drachmas, is much too small to represent the loan on the security of the items that precede it, or even the interest.

michigan.apis.1850.s: Most of the surviving portion of this letter is concerned with mundane business transactions. The writer acknowledges the receipt of 24 drachmas by the hand of a certain Satrios. He reports that, probably upon written request, he has put in an order for a mattress and some dry goods, which are not yet ready.Their combined cost (52 drachmas ?) exceeds the amount brought by Satrios, and this is a source of concern for the writer. He promises to make up the difference from his own pocket, although he is not affluent. He mentions also that he has bought two artabas of lentils (the price is not given) and that Satrios is unwilling to take them with him. Near the end of the business portion of the letter the writer requests a cloak, to be made by his mother.

michigan.apis.1854.t: marriage agreement and donatio mortis causa
michigan.apis.1854.s: This text has two parts. The first (lines 1-8) is the end of a Greek marriage agreement, referred to as syngraphe. The surviving part of the marriage contract contains arrangements for the repayment of dowry in case of divorce and a provision ensuring that one party may retain control over property acquired after the date of the present agreement. Although the majority of such contracts were arranged by the husband and wife themselves, the parties in this settlement are both women. Apollonous, who undertakes the agreement (line 5), is responsible for returning the dowry in case of divorce (lines 1-4) and is liable to prosecution in event of default (lines 5-6). She operates on behalf of the husband in the marriage, and is presumably his mother. The second party is not clearly identified in the remaining fragment, but appears to be Tamarres (see lines 822n). The identity of the spouses whose marriage is at issue is also a matter of conjunction. They are evidently Kronous, a beneficiary of Tamarres (lines 11-20) and therefore probably her daughter, and Gaius Julius Isidoros: the names of these two are linked once in the marriage agreement (line 6), and one or both of them also appear in the division of property in contexts that make it practically certain that they are man and wife (lines 11, 20).;Lines 8-22 contain Tamarres' distribution of property. Her dispositions consist of at least three parcels of land (including one of 16 arouras: lines 12, 17, 18; also 19?) and a slave (lines 14-15), and provide for a payment to the household of Kronous. The text concludes with provisions for the alimentary support of the donor (line 21), and the name and the beginning of the signalments of the hypographeus. In the lost second column would have been the subjectively phrased subscriptions of Apollonous and Tamarres and the signatures of the hypographeus and the witnesses, if any.

michigan.apis.1928.s: McMillan in ed. princ.: Although the text preserves only a dating formula, the fact that it is written in a literary hand strongly suggests that the text is from a martyrology, where formulas of this type are common. They may occur at the beginning or end of a martyrology. Since the text does not continue on the verso, we may assume that the piece is the last page of the codex. The mention of Diocletian in l 1 and Clodius Culcianus in l. 4 gives further evidence to support the supposition that this fragment is from a martyrology. Both of these men are mentioned by name in several martyrologies. The date mentioned in the text is: December 18, 307 A.D.;PJS in BASP 31, 1994, pp. 121-124: There is writing on the other side of the papyrus, which seems to be unrelated to the text siscussed here. The writing on the back stands upside down in relation to the main text, Coptic?;Finally, PJS proposes that it is the end of a parchment codex which once contained the Passion of Saint Dioskorus.

michigan.apis.1967.s: Zoilos writes to his mother Theodora to inform her that his sister is very ill and that she might give birth to a baby on that day after only 7 months of pregnancy. Meanwhile, Zoilos reports, the sister's husband has left the city to go to Oxyrhynchos to work off an inescapable obligation. Zoilos urges his mother to provide accomodation there for him and his co-workers.

michigan.apis.1969.s: Dionysios writes to Hermes and Dioskoras concerning a matter of business.Dionysios appears to be general manager of extensive properties belonging to Theodora. He writes to two of his subordinates, who are described on the verso as estate managers (phrontistai). He has heard that the year's crop are going at very low prices, and wheat specifically in their locality at 12 drachmas per artaba. Since Theodora wishes them to buy up as much wheat as they can, Dionysius instructs them to spend two talents for this purpose. The only condition he imposes is that what they obtain in this way be "good clean seed."

The docket on the verso strongly suggests that the certificate on the recto was requested by their son Julius to prove his own eligibility to this privileged class within the Alexandrian and Egyptian society.

michigan.apis.1980.s: This letter from an unnamed writer to his mother is devoted for the most part to greetings sent to members of the family. These are interrupted only by an urgent request for provisions and medicaments and an expression of anxiety about an anticipated visit of the writer's sister. The verso contains the address (house of Apa Kyri in the amphodon of Hierakeion). The family is clearly Christian, and the author's use of the proskynema formula, a pagan one, shows that the writer was a new convert from paganism continuing old mental habits.

michigan.apis.1991.s: Hugh Lloyd-Jones' note "Two people seem to have made an agreement involving the horses given by Zeus to Tros. Were these people Laomedon and Heracles, or a representative of Herakles? There is not enough of the text to make it woth while to speculate about the content. But we have found nothing here that Callimachus could not have written; and we have noticed several homericisms of just the kind we expect from him or one of his contemporaries. I Think the fragmnet deserves a place among the Dubia of the next edition of Callimachus"

These animals include some donkeys and one ass. The purpose for sending these animals was to enable Koryphos to come after some ropes for the vineyards. The animals, of course, would be used to transport the ropes.

michigan.apis.2020.s: The papyrus contains a letter to the strategoi and royal scribes of the Eptanomoi and the Arsinoite, giving instructions concerning preparations for a visit of Severus Alexander and his mother, Iulia Mamaea. It apparently reinforces a previous communication from the epistrategos, refers to a schedule of requisitions previously sent to the same officials and which they are now instructed to post up in public places, and insists that all requisitions are to be made within the proper limits only, severe penalties being threatened if the officials are caught overstepping the mark.

michigan.apis.2023.s: The writer, in an abrupt style, refers to a variety of things - his delay in loading camels, lentils and their current local cost, grain and fish. He informs Horion, whom he addresses in a slightly superior tone, that he is sending one basket containing jujubes, pomegranates, and gourds, and another with fresh dates, some old wine secured with difficulty, and a quantity of bones. After expressing the customary greetings, he reverts to business details - his failure to receive the cotton chiton he wanted, his readiness to have one woven for Horion provided materials and measurements are sent, grain being being sent to Psobthis, and the dispatch of dates, pomegranates, and a letter through Phatres, who acts as a go-between.
michigan.apis.2023.luogo: Oxyrhynchite nome, Middle Egypt, province of Egypt (?)

The tasks mentioned in the lines which survive, are cleaning, digging, and pruning, all performed in connection with vineyards.

michigan.apis.2047.s: Homer, Odyssey 21.168-176. The text is fully vulgate with the exception of the substitution of (apparently) a present or aorist active participle for the substantive "mnesteres" in 174, corrected by M. 2;173: "oiston": the dot over iota is intended as a diaeresis mark.;174: 'mnesteres a]gauoi' tacha therapo]ntes aga[uoi: what M. 1 actually wrote is not recoverable. It may have been either the presentactive participle of "mnesteuw, mnesteuontes", which mdoes not occur in Homer, or the aorist active participle, "mnesteusantes", which occurs only at Od. 4.684. Either of these would give a meaning reasonably close to that of the vulgate text (m. 2's correction supra is apparently vulagte); but each would corrupt the meter. At Il. 19.281, we read "therapontes agauoi" in the same position as "mnesteres agauoi" here. It is possible then that m. 1 wrote the phrase from Iliad as a reminiscent variant; the phrase has at least the advantage of fitting the meter.

michigan.apis.2061.s: The text is a series of biblical quotations followed by an allegorical interpretation. These quotations are taken from Matthew (two), John (one), Luke (one) and the Proverbs (fifteen). These selections do not seem to be based on any principle. There is certainly nouniform theme that would connect them. The passages from the Proverbs come from the chapters X to XVIII, most of them from chapters XIV, XV, and XVI. The four groups are separated from each other by captions. In three instances these titles do not serve their purpose, because they are incorporated into the last line of the preceding group and thus not recognizable without difficulty.
michigan.apis.2061.luogo: Oxyrhynchos, Oxyrhynchite nome, Middle Egypt, province of Egypt (?)

michigan.apis.2072.s: This papyrus contains a survey of expenditure (cf. line 26) and probably of revenues also. However, the remains of the first column do not suggest receipts but also expenditures. There are frequent references to the production of cloth and clothing, and there are expenses for dying and fulling (cp. SB XVI 12314). However, there are also amounts paid out for wages and foodstuffs listed.

michigan.apis.2073.s: The text is a bill of loading for certain articles placed on board a boat, and includes money, clothing and food. It may be compared with P. Oxy. XVI 1923 (V or early VI cent.), an inventory of utensils and food placed on a boat, probably, the editors suggest, for use on a proposed voyage.

Probably because there are now difficulties after Kepion's death concerning this room, Hestiodorus addresses the defensor civitatis.

In some cases two or three persons are grouped together but elsewhere a single person is mentioned. The purpose of this papyrus can no longer be established.

michigan.apis.2096.s: Only the right part of this letter has been preserved and the missing section makes our understanding of the text tentative and translation impossible. It is, however, clear that the writer complains that he has been deserted by his companions and would have been alone somewhere had he not forced a certain Enoch to stay with him. He asks the addressee for an iron tool and a ship to transport something. He also asks the recipient of the letter to reply.

michigan.apis.2115.s: This papyrus contains portions of two columns of a text which mentions among other things a love affair, events connected with a spring, and devouring by beasts. The goddess Aphrodite is mentioned early in the fragment, and two names of mortal persons, Pamphilos and Eurydike, can be read with certainty. The greater part of what survives is apparently narrative in the third person, but instances of the first person and of direct adress occur.
michigan.apis.2115.luogo: Oxyrhynchos, Oxyrhynchite nome, Middle Egypt, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2116.s: This papyrus contains a fragment of a letter concerned with small private affairs. The names of both the sender and the recipient are lost. The letter was written in Alexandria. The content of the letter is without importance, but it has in line 2 another example of thyris to designate a wall niche or cupboard.
michigan.apis.2116.luogo: Oxyrhynchos, Oxyrhynchite nome, Middle Egypt, province of Egypt (?)

michigan.apis.2117.t: Request for Appointment of a Guardian
michigan.apis.2117.s: (Copy of a) petition to the prefect, to whom Aurelia Diodora requests to appoint Aurelius Theon as her legal guardian. The petition itself is in Latin, but is followed by a subscription of the petitioner and by the consentment of the future guardian, both in Greek; the approval note of the prefect, again in Latin, concludes the text. As the petition and the prefect's approval are in the same hand, the text is probably a copy restituted to Aurelia Diodora, while the original was kept in the prefect's files.
michigan.apis.2117.luogo: Oxyrhynchus, Oxyrhynchite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2118.s: Private letter in which Phileas sends greetings to his wife Cyrilla and other family members. Noteworthy is a proskynemaformula directed to Apollo.

michigan.apis.2134.s: The text on this papyrus is concerned with a verbal court process. The date, the commands from the prefect or from the preses and, probably, the announcements of the speeches given by the two parties or their advocates were in Latin, but the words of the parties or their advocates were in Greek, following standard practice. Unfortunately, the text is too fragmentary to establish the object of the process, and the Greek is so badly preserved that no more than a literal transcription of readable passages is possible.

According to l. 24 the original letter of which this text is a copy, although addresses to the nome exactor, was turned over to one of the epimeletai who supervised the shipment as a receipt. Nonetheless, the present papyrus plainly did not remain in the Alexandrian office.;In addition to the docket (26-27), the back contains two short accounts which have no connection with the main text. The first is dated to a fifth indiction, presumably A.D. 376/7. As a sample, l. 3, " from Kopreus and his brothers, on account of rent 31 1/2 art., on account of arrears 7 art., interest 2 1/3 art., together 40 5/6 art". From the second account, which follows in the same hand after a blank space of 6 cm: (l. 9) "of these 13 art. were brought up to the city by Kopreus on Mesore 25".

Expenses in terms of money were itemized at the right side of the text line by line, but these figures have been stripped away. Their total, however, is presented in the last line of the column.

michigan.apis.2353.s: The papyrus preserves part of a poem which was put to use as a writing exercise. The format is familiar: a teacher supplies a writing model and a pupil's copy follows. Here the pupil fails to finish his assignment. He stops writing before quite completing to copy the first verse in line 5.;Each of the three complete hexameters in the writing model deals with a different mythological event. The lines are arranged so as to form an alphabetical acrostic. We know of numerous such abecadaria designed to aid in the teaching of various subjects, and one of them closely resembles our text in that it deals with mythological subjects as well. It is recorded in the 'Notebook of Papnouthion", lines 18-37. Formally, it differs from the present poem in three ways. First, it is written in iambic trimeters, rather than hexameters; second, the alphabetic pattern is alpha omega, beta psi, gamma chi etc.; and finally, these pairs of verses, rather than individual hexameters, each treat an incident in myth or legend.

michigan.apis.2495.s: The text contains the beginning of a Sahidic translation of the Panegyric of Gregory of Nazianzus on Basil of Caesarea (for the Greek original, see Migne, PG XXXVI 493ff). The Coptic translator has often had recourse to loose paraphrase instead of verbatim rendition, and he may not always have understood his model. The introductory section (R i 1-24), set off by an elaborate border, is a considerable expansion of the Greek title.

michigan.apis.2503.s: The testator, whose name is lost, is a son of Didas and Dioskorous and grandson of Didymos. His two sons, Ammmonios and Herakleides, share equally in the estate, which consists of one aroura of vineyard, and the half share of a house and a courtyard held in joint ownership with the testator's brother, Moschion. The right to reside on the property and to have the services of the slaves bequeathed by her husband is secured to the wife, Kleopatra, for as long as she lives and remains unmarried. Provisions for the burial of the father are unusually detailed, but unfortunately they fall in the most mutilated portion of the papyrus. The amount of money to be spent, not less than two hundred drachmas, is designated, as well as the place where the body is presumably to be interred, near the Labyrinth.

michigan.apis.2505.s: The text is too defective to permit a detailed analysis of the terms of the agreement. The settlement of property is almost completely lost, but it includes land, a house and court, and personal property which is described in more detail than usual. There is provision for the payment of debts that may still be due on the death of the donor. The text also provides for the care of the son till he becomes of age and apparently stipulate that the mother may reside on the property with her son as long as she lives. No guardian is provided. Peteeus reserves control of the property during his lifetime.

michigan.apis.2513.s: Tamystha, daughter of Apollonios, makes a testamentary division of her property to take effect after her death. Her brother Satabous acts as her guardian in the transaction, her husband being dead. The property consists chiefly of the half share of a house, which was purchased from Ptolemais, Didis, and a third party whose name is lost, and which is apparently held in common with the sellers without division. This house and the personal and household effects of Tamystha are left to her daughter Taorsenouphis. Two stipulations are added, one that Taorsenouphis shall provide a fitting burial for her mother, and the other that she shall also pay the sum of twenty silver drachmas to her brother Heron.

michigan.apis.2538.s: Fragments from a column of the Odyssey, which contained the end of Book XIV and the first lines of Book XV;The Michigan text presents one variant reading unrecorded elsewhere (514). Its omission of ll. 14.515-517 is in agreement with parts of the tradition.;514: "paidi": vulg. "photi". The variant is unattested elsewhere. "paidi" and metrically equivalent forms as "pais" occur very frequently in Homer at this place in the line, but only once is a form of this word followed by a form of "ekastos" (Il. 23.350). But there the words are in different cases, and the place in the line is different. It seems likely then that the reading here is a true variant and not a reminiscence. However, it is clear that "photi" is the better reading, although it could be argued that "pais" here refers to the condition of the men in question. They are slaves, and Eumaios' reference to them as "paides" would be in accordance with later usage. Both Aeschylus and Aristophanes, among others, use "pais" to refer to a slave {cf. Aeschylus, Choephoroi 653; Aristophanes, Archanians 395; Clouds 132; also Epicrates, fr. 5.2, Demosthenes 33.8];515-517 om.: About two-thirds of the MSS of Od. omit these lines; cf. OCT, ap. crit., ad loc. The lines are repeated almost exactly at Od. 15.337-339. Aristarchus athetised the lines in Book 14, but apparentlynotin Book 15 [M. van der Valk defends the lines; op. cit. (Odyssey). 188]. The lines are clearly necessary at both places.;520: "katelekt{o} [ep]i: scriptio plena;533: "gl]aphure . . . ioge": reda "glaphurei . . . iogei".;post 533: The ink markson two levels below the title "ODUSSEIAS" are faint but definetely ink, not dirt. On the first level, there is a horizontal dash beneath the letters "eia". This corresponds to the dash above those letters. On the second level, there are two obliques, the first from bottom left to top right and the second from top left to bottom right; the first oblique is at such a wide angle from line-level as to be almost perpendicular; the second is at an angle of about 45 degress. The letter may be delta. A lacuna before it may have held iota. If this is correct, the letters identify the book which ends above the title, "i]d" (=14). It is also possible that the extant letter is epsilon. This would make the reading i]e (=15), identifying the book which begins below the title. But the shape of the letter does not fit epsilon well, and its angularity contrasts sharply nwith the roundness of epsilon in "Odusseias" above. Cf. P.Oxy. 15.1817 (Il. 18.617 ff.) for the book title following the last line of the book [see P.Cornell XII = P.Oxy. III 548, Il. 9.235-301, introd.);1 marg.: The coronis above and to left of line 1 marks the beginning of the book.;2. "ochet": read "oichet"; rec. "oichet". The use of the regular imperfect instead of the epic is common in both the papyri (cf. P.Ryl. 1.53 ad loc.) and the MSS. ;5: "e[udo]nt{e}: the second epsilon is very uncertain. Scriptio plena.

michigan.apis.2603.s: The text deals with medicine rather than magic; for the medicamenta, irrational as they appear to us, are the sole means of treatment. There are no prayers or spells. The line of demarcation between medicine and magic is, of course, not always easily drawn. Prayers, spells and substances are all applied in the same pragmatic way.;A certain arrangement is discernable. Page 167 deals with wounds, hemorrhages and swellings; page 168, with digestive disorders. The remedy for toothache is interpolated, because the roasted dove brings to mind the "dove-herb."

michigan.apis.2766.s: Hypothesis to the first Hippolytos of Euripides

michigan.apis.2767.s: The text is a receipt issued to Aphthonios, son of Herakion, who was almost certainly an epimeletes annones, by Ptolemaios, official distributor of provisions to military units (diadotes). He acknowledges receipt of 150 sextarii of pickled meat, to be delivered to the numerus Transtigritanorum in the Arsinoite nome.
michigan.apis.2767.luogo: Oxyrhynchos, Oxyrhynchite nome, Middle Egypt, Middle Egypt (?)

michigan.apis.2769.s: Contract whereby a woman, Thenarmaeis, daughter of Petesouchos, binds herself not to go to law with her brothers Harmaeis and Petesouchos over their paternal inheritance; the sheet bears, from top to bottom: 1) a short date; 2) the regular introductory formula, giving the date in full and the place where the contract was drawn up; 3) the registration docket of the grapheion (record office); 4) the subscription of the principal party, which resumes the terms of the agreement, allowing the scribe to leave the body of the contract unwritten; on the verso was the title of the document
michigan.apis.2769.luogo: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2771.s: the text consists of a fragment of a catalogue of women
michigan.apis.2771.sup: 1 papyrus ; frg. 1: 6 x 10.2 cm.; frg. 2: 3.5 x 8.2 cm.; frg. 3:2.8 x 5.8 cm.

michigan.apis.2772.s: Commentary on Aitia. Lines 1-7 seem to be concerned with Apollo, l. 8 is vacant and lines 9-24 probably contain a prose narration about king Teuthis and a statue of Athena with bandaged thigh.
michigan.apis.2772.sup: 2 papyri ; fr. 1: 18.5 x 7.3 cm; fr. 2: 3.2 x 2.5 cm

michigan.apis.2776.s: Alimentary contract, consisting of a property settlement entered into by [- - -] the elder, son of Harmiysis, and his wife . . ., daughter of Orseus, fixing the sum which the husband is obliged to pay to his wife in case of his divorcing her and describing the real properties which would become sureties for the payment of this sum
michigan.apis.2776.luogo: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2777.s: Fragmentary petition from a certain Aurelius Heron, who has been compelled to take up for the second time the office of horiodeiktes(?), following the death of the man who had held the post after him
michigan.apis.2777.dt: IIIrd century A.D., not later than 277/278 A.D. (April 26)

michigan.apis.2780.t: Sale of Part of a House
michigan.apis.2780.s: Demotic contract for the sale of a third of a house and courtyard, made by Tasouchos, daughter of Sekonopis, to Patynis, son of Harapis; the subscriptions are in Greek, as well as the date which was added at the top of the papyrus
michigan.apis.2780.luogo: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt
k: Talei, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome; canal of Moeris

michigan.apis.2782.t: Contract of Sale of Vacant Lots
michigan.apis.2782.s: Copy of the docket, the signatures and the abstract of a (demotic?) contract by which Kronion, son of Patynis, sells the vacant lots belonging to him in Talei to Pimos, son of Orsenouphis
michigan.apis.2782.luogo: either Talei or Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2786.s: Petition, addressed to Apollonios, strategos of the division of Polemon, by at least two men, against a local informer against whom several complaints had already been filed, and who is here accused of having forced a man to suicide by his machinations
michigan.apis.2786.luogo: Probably Tebtynis (or a village in the area), Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2787.s: Register presenting the substance of the declarations of the current census in topographical order
michigan.apis.2787.luogo: Karanis, Herakleidou meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2788.s: Contract by which Herakles, son of Chairemon, also called Mieus, cedes to Chairemon, also called Onnophris, son of Horion, five arourai of catoecic land near Tebtynis; at the top of the papyrus are the brief descriptions of the parties concerned; on the verso, a brief docket
michigan.apis.2788.luogo: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt
k: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome; Makedon; ta Ammegina legomena; he Kanabis legomene

michigan.apis.2789.t: Application for Lease of Grain Land
michigan.apis.2789.s: Offer, made by Kastor son of Kopres to Chairemon son of Polydeukes, to lease for three years some catoecic land near Kerkesoucha
michigan.apis.2789.luogo: probably either Kerkesoucha or Karanis, Herakleidou meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2791.s: Copy of a contract by which Chairemon, son of Horos, Herodes, son of Herodes, and Patynis, son of Marepsemis, agree to admit Papnebtynis, son of Petesis, as a partner with a quarter interest in a four-year lease of a catoecic allotment of 40 arourai rented to them by Chairemon, son of Penkios
michigan.apis.2791.luogo: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt
k: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome; Perses

michigan.apis.2793.t: Lease of a Reed Bed on Waste Land
michigan.apis.2793.s: Contract by which Herakleides the younger, son of Herakleides, leases to Kronion, son of Hera[- - -], a reed bed on waste land; the lessee is expected to break down the soil of this land overgrown with reeds and to restore it to cultivation, for which he is to receive a cash subvention from the lessor. The note in l. 1 is an order to file this copy of the contract in the grapheion archives.
michigan.apis.2793.luogo: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt
k: [Tebtynis(?), Polemonos] meris, Arsinoite nome; Ibion Eikosipentarouron

michigan.apis.2801.s: Request, sent by an higher official, probably to the komogrammateus of Karanis, about the status of a certain Ptolemaios, who claimed to have some privileges, including the right to marry an Antinoite woman

michigan.apis.2802.s: Contract by which Haryotes, son of Haryotes, leases to Paopis, son of Orseus, to Orseus, son of Paopis, and to Semenis, son of Haryotes, twenty-six arourai of a catoecic allotment
michigan.apis.2802.luogo: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2806.s: Fragment of philosophical reflections on the relations between myth and nature, mentioning myths used for natural phenomena: identification of Artemis as the moon(?), abduction of Kore by Plouton(?)

michigan.apis.2807.s: List of body parts (eyes, ears, cheeks, noses and shoulder), perhaps from a medical text or from a mythological (school?) text showing Hephaistos modeling Pandora

michigan.apis.2811.s: Contract by which Sokrates, son of Ptolemaios, leases to Horos, son of Horos, four arourai of a catoecic allotment near Theogonis
michigan.apis.2811.luogo: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt
k: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome; Theogonis; Perses

michigan.apis.2814.luogo: Probably Karanis, Herakleidou meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2817.s: Subscriptions to a contract by which Herodes, also called Orseus the younger, son of Herodes, sells to Didymos the elder, son of Lysimachos, a catoecic allotment of three arourai near Tebtynis
michigan.apis.2817.luogo: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2820.t: Sale of Part of a House
michigan.apis.2820.s: Subscriptions to a contract by which Didyme, daughter of Petesouchos, sells to Marres, son of Dionysios, her share of a three-story house in Talei; at the top of the papyrus is the date; a blank space of 18 cm was left to write the body of the contract
michigan.apis.2820.luogo: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2822.s: Fragment of a report made for or after a land inspection (episkepsis), aimed at checking what land was uninundated

michigan.apis.2825.s: Subscription to a contract by which Harpaesis, son of Panorses, agrees to plant mulberry trees on the dykes around 300 arourai of land, and to provide up to 150 trees, which he agrees to water five times a month. At the top of the papyrus, the body of the contract was begun, but left unfinished, probably because of a mistake in the second word
michigan.apis.2825.luogo: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2827.s: Contract by which Horos the elder, son of Apollonios, leases to Ptolemaios, son of Apion, five arourai of the public estates which Horos himself is farming, for one year; at the bottom of the sheet are a docket of the grapheion recording the registration of the lease and a memorandum of the clerk, giving the descriptions of the contracting parties.
michigan.apis.2827.luogo: Talei, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt
k: Talei, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome; Perses; Theogonis; hai Meleleutos legomenai

michigan.apis.2828.s: Contract for the lease, for three years, of a bath and an adjoining chaff bin on the property owned jointly by two Romans of equestrian rank, in the vicinity of Theogonis; the lessor, Herakleides, son of Isidoros, the collector or bailiff of the estate, unertakes to pay the taxes on the bath, while the lessees, Diodoros, son of Euphranor, and Patynis the younger, son of Philon, are to pay a rent of 265 artabai of wheat, as well as the operating expenses of the bath
michigan.apis.2828.luogo: Talei, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt
k: Talei, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome; Theogonis; Perses

michigan.apis.2829.s: This text contains a list of payments of an unspecified nature. There is no indication of what the payment consists, but presumably the sums listed refer to drachmas. Also there is no indication of the person(s) to whom or by whom the payments were made.

michigan.apis.2830.s: Contract by which Cheos, son of Harmiysis, sells to Mieus, son of Phomsais, three arourai of sacred land; this copy was intended for incorporation in the records of the grapheion (as shown by l. 1), and bears a brief docket on the verso.
michigan.apis.2830.luogo: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt
k: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome; kyte (koite?) legomene

michigan.apis.2831.s: Contract, lacking the customary heading and the subscriptions of the contracting parties, by which Didymos the younger, son of Lysimachos, acknowledges to his wife and sister Hero the cession of 10 arourai of a catoecic allotment near Theogonis, cession which was actually made on May 25, 33 A.D., and by which Hero agrees to a valuation of part of her dowry, which is to be given to Didymos to complete the price of the 10 arourai
michigan.apis.2831.luogo: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2832.s: Fragment of a contract for the division of property consisting of both land and slaves
michigan.apis.2832.luogo: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2833.sup: 2 papyri ; Fr. I: 13, 5 x 12 cm; Fr. II: 9.5 x 4.5 cm

michigan.apis.2834.luogo: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2836.luogo: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2837.s: Receipt for delivery of wheat made in the name of sitologoi of Karanis by Pnas
michigan.apis.2837.luogo: unknown harbor, Memphite or Herakleopolite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2838.s: Receipt for delivery of wheat made in the name of sitologoi of Karanis by Pnas
michigan.apis.2838.luogo: unknown harbor, Memphite or Herakleopolite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2840.luogo: unknown harbor, Herakleopolite or Memphite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2843.s: Lease of pasture land by Herakleides, son of Didymos, from the six elders and the secretary of the public cultivators in Tebtynis (compare P.Mich. II, 121, recto, col. IV, abstract 12). The body of the contract was not finished
michigan.apis.2843.luogo: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2848.luogo: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2851.s: Request from Herodes, also called Herakleides, to Kronion, the notary of Tebtynis, concerning 13 1/2 arourai of catoecic land that Herodes has previously ceded to Herakleides the younger, son of Maron; the object of the request is lost, but it could have been written to support Herakleides's vain effort to obtain the deed of cession without the necessary authorization, which he had lost (see also P.Mich. V, 353, of 48 A.D.)
michigan.apis.2851.luogo: probably Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2852.s: Copy of a return addressed by Petheus the elder son of Petheus to the bibliophylax Thrakidas, declaring his properties in and near Karanis and near Kerkesoucha
michigan.apis.2852.luogo: Karanis, Herakleidou meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt
k: Arsinoite nome; Karanis; Herakleidou meris; ousia (former estate) of Germanicus; Psenarpsenesis; Kerkesoucha

michigan.apis.2853.luogo: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2860.luogo: Karanis, Herakleidou meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2861.s: End of a contract of uncertain character, perhaps a loan of grain, or possibly a lease of land with rent in kind
michigan.apis.2861.luogo: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2863.s: Receipt issued to Harmais alias Pelkis, son of Harmais, for payment of the transfer tax on the purchase of a half share of a house at the bank of the nomarchy at Arsinoiton polis to the farmers of the tax in the nomarchy
michigan.apis.2863.luogo: Arsinoiton polis, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt
k: Ptolemais Euergetis (Arsinoiton polis), Arsinoite nome; Ptolemaiou nomarchia; Tebtynis, Polemonos meris

michigan.apis.2864.luogo: either Karanis of unknown harbor, Memphite or Herakleopolite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2865.luogo: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2870.s: Acknowledgment by Ptolemaios, son of Ptolemaios, that he has received from Kronion, nomographos of Tebtynis, a deed of cession prepared throught the agency of Kronion for the sons of Heron, son of Labion, who have conveyed some property to Ptolemaios
michigan.apis.2870.luogo: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2871.s: Marriage contract in the form of a bank draft, by which is acknowledged that the husband has received his wife's dowry

michigan.apis.2875.t: Receipt for Part of a Dowry
michigan.apis.2875.s: Subscription to a deed by which Haryotes, son of Herodion, acknowledges the receipt of 100 silver drachmai from his wife Taorsenouphis, daughter of Aphrodisios, as an additional gift beyond the dowry and the parapherna received previously; in case of separation the money is to be returned. The transaction is recorded in the grapheion registers P.Mich. II, 128, col. III, l. 5; V, 240, l. 26
michigan.apis.2875.luogo: Tebtynis, Polemonos meris, Arsinoite nome, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.2876.s: Ordinance issued by the association of the salt merchants of Tebtynis, appointing one of them to be their supervisor and to collect and pay the public dues for which they are liable after having obtained the monopolistic concession of the sale of salt in Tebtynis and some neighboring villages; it also defines the territory in which all members may sell salt and the areas reserved for certain individual members; fixes the sale prices for the various grades of salt; provides for a monthly meeting; and establishes penalties for breach of the regulations.

michigan.apis.2913.s: Diogenes writes to his brother Dorion concerning the high prices on olive oil in his brother's village. The price is not indicated in the letter. Diogenes further states his opininion that olive oil should not be purchased at such a high rate.

michigan.apis.2914.s: A single column, numbered 18, of a roll containing a medical catechism. It contains the end of the answer to a question now lost, a new question, and the beginning of its answer. The first question in all probability asked for the properties of olive oil, that made from unripe olives,and that made from fully ripe olives, and the powers of each. The second question -"What is the best time for a catabrocation?- concerns illnesses characterized by paroxysms. Reminiscent of our questions are those found in Orib., Coll. Med. vi 12, 15; vii 1, 2, 5-12, 23, 24; viii 1, 4, 6, 34, 38; et. al.
michigan.apis.2914.dt: (second half of the) IInd century A.D.

michigan.apis.2915.s: It betrays a preoccupation with linen-weaving and is much enchanced by the partly obscure reflections on the moral responsibility of the recipient as a linen-weaver

michigan.apis.2916.s: This papyrus contains a letter to Phanias, a secretary of the Harbor of Memphis, concerning business matters. The writer mentions some wine and plants which he put on board a ship for Phanias, and tells him to remind two other persons about a matter, apparently a payment due.

michigan.apis.2937.t: Dictionary of metamorphosed characters from myth
michigan.apis.2937.s: A mythological dictionary. The five nearly complete entries in Column II all concern metamorphosed characters in Greek myth whose names begin with "alpha", but they are not ordered according to any stricter rules of alphabetization. Two of these entries cite the Hesiodic Catalogue of Women, the Ethoiae, as their authorities. A Third cites simply "Hesiod", and a fourth entry refers to an unknown passage of Aeschylus.;The scanty remains of col. I apparently represent three entries having eight, eleven and three lines respectively preserved.
michigan.apis.2937.dt: (late) IInd century A.D. / IIIrd century A.D.

michigan.apis.2959.s: The damage to the papyrus and the resulting damage to the text prevents a certain conclusion regarding the content of this text. From line 2 (salutem) It is clear that the text had the form of a letter, but other words make it clear that this was hardly a private letter. This text may therefore be an official letter, which may be concerned with legionnary veterans (lines 4 and 9). In that case, this text can only be a copy emanating from a perhaps military office of significant rank.

michigan.apis.2962.s: As is so often the case, the essential point of the letter remains unintelligible while the rest of the letter is clear enough. There is an ellipsis or omission in line 4. The use of the title Dux as late as the VIIIth century is interisting.

michigan.apis.2969.s: Taurinos writes to his "father" of his prosperity, evidenced by the great quantity of fruit and wine sent to the drying place, and invites him to come visit him. The drying place was used for drying fruit and fermenting wine. Verso b was written before verso a and has no apparent relation to it or to recto. It is probably the beginning of a long letter, to judge from the size of the characters, from which a small strip was torn for the reception of recto.

Neither the number of camels needed nor the job for which they are needed are specified in the letter.

A narrow (unpublished) strip of papyrus with the larger piece may be part of the preceding column; the few legible letters seem to be in the same hand.

michigan.apis.2991.s: This papyrus contains a list of names arranged by families, which suggests that the list was compiled from a census list. Some persons listed within certain name-group have no apparent relation to eachother; probably these persons were grouped together because they shared a house. Lines 140-145 (verso, col. iii) contain 31 numbers, all in the region between 19 through 23. The total sum of these figures is then given in line 146. This construction follows a standard formula: A sum is given, then specified, and finally the single entries of the analysis are added up once again as a final check.

michigan.apis.3009.s: Settlement made out of court by, on the one hand, Apollos (deceased), Paulos and Maria, children and heirs of a certain Ioannes (John), represented by the presbyter Victor, son of Besarion, and by Senouthes, son of Apollos, and.on the other hand, Psaios, son of Mousaios, and his wife Talous, daughter of Herakleios. Several issues were at stake between them: the price of several holdings bought by Ioannes to Psaios and his wife, and its payment; taxes collected by Apollos on Psaios, allegedly wrongfully; and a house pledged by Psaios for the sake of the defending party in connection with a court fee.

The collocation of dues paid in money and in kind suggests an account prepared by the supervisory bureau of the nome, to which the diverse local agencies responsible for their collection submitted reports.

michigan.apis.3028.s: Notarial deed by which a dispute is settled between Aurelius Nikantinoos on the one hand and Aurelius Phoibammon and his wife Aurelia Anastasia alias Tekrompia, represented by Anastasia's uncle, Apollos son of Dioskoros, on the other hand, concerning a piece of land. This was originally owned by Nikantinoos's parents, who used it to secure a loan from Iosephios and his parents; this liability went to their heirs, including Nikantinoos, while the property itself was inherited by Nikantinoos's nephew and nieces, and then sold by them to Phoibammon and Anastasia. The settlement, made with the advice of mediators, is that Phoibammon and Anastasia pay an indemnity in cash and in kind to Nikantinoos for paying the mortgage on this piece of land and ratifying the sale

The question of the identity of the criminals is not debated, nor is there any call for a court settlement of the matter.

michigan.apis.3117.s: The diptych contains a series of accounts which for the most port deal with a series of harvest operation-reaping an threshing-carried out between Pauni 2 and Epeiph 30. In addition there three short entries, the relation of which to the foregoing is not clear. This was probably a day-book of an overseer, who kept thereon a detailed record of the daily work performed by the various laborers employed on the estates under his supervision. This record he would use as a memorandum for the calculation of the wages to be paid these workmen, and also for the compilation of a report of expenditures to be presented to his employer, the owner or lessee of the estates, cf. e. g. P. Lond. III1170 verso.

michigan.apis.3118.s: Side 1: Syllabary, first a col. of vowels, then combinations with consonants. In col. 7 iota functions both as consonant and as vowel.;Side 2: Alphabet in regular and reverse order, then the letters are paired.
k: Greek language, Hellenistic (300 B.C.-600 A.D.)--Writing;vProblems, exercises, etc.

michigan.apis.3119.s: Side 1 contains a column of 21 proper names on the left side and two drawings on the right side. The first drawing represents a head with spiky hair. The second depicts a whole stick figure with large round eyes and a body covered by the same short strokes that are used to represent the hair on the head. Side 2 contains a mathematical exercise.

michigan.apis.3145.s: Five columns remain from what was once a much larger record -the collections of poll tax owed by taxpaying male peasants of the Fayum village of Philadelphia who were between the ages of 14 and 62 for the fourth regnal year of the emperor Gaius. The ledger was one of about 150 papyri that were assembled by the collector of catitation taxes in the Fayyum village of Philadelphia from late in the reign of Tiberius to the middle years of the reign of Nero. This year ledger was laid out by a "katandragraphos" (m. 1), a professional scribe whose specialty was to draft itemized tax records; he wrote out the names of the individual taxpayers together with patronymics and other pertinent information, such a profession (line 41) or current place orf residence (line 27). He positioned the entries so that less space was allotted to men labelled "apolysimoi" (e.g. col. ii, line 44), because their entries routinely consisted of a single line. These more privileged villagers collected poll tax amonng themselves and were not visited by the tax collector month after month; hence no record of instalments folloed under the names of apolysimoi and less space was left between an entry fo an apolysimos and the following entry.;The taxpayers mentioned in the surviving five columns of this year ledger for 39/40 have bames beginning with the letter alpha, and the year ledger folloed an alphabetical arrangement. After the "katandragraphos" laid out the ledger, he verified his work against his original list, drawing a short, thick stroke above the middle of each entry. Two other scribes (m. 2 and m. 3) then recorded the payments the individuals made in the course of the year 39/40. The two strokes extending toward and into the left margin below the taxpayers's name indicate that a taxpayer had paid in full for the year; seven of the taxpayers listed in col. ii had the strokes drawn in front of their names, while a single stroke was drawn in front of the name of the eighth, an apolysimos. The poll taxes whose payments are recorded in this roll are for syntaximon, the laographia paid at its highest rate of 44 drachmai; the instalments were invariably 4 dr. or multiples of 4 dr., showing that the goverment's issue of tetradrachms was the currency required for such payments. A small surcharge (6 chalkoi) was usually paid with the final instalment for syntaximon/laographia, together with pig tax ("uike") of one drachma and one obol.

michigan.apis.3159.t: Fragment of a Homer-Hypothesis with no gods
michigan.apis.3159.s: The papyrus contains a prose summary of the seventh and eigth books of the Iliad which is unlike extant Homer-hypotheses in manuscripts or on papyri in two respects. First, it quotes not only the first line of each book, as papyrus hypotheses do regularly, but also the last line. Second, the hypothesis omits all mention of gods. Deities play a minor role in these books, so it is conceivable that the hypothesizer could have left them out here, because of their lack of importance to the narrative, but still have included them in his hypotheses of e.g. A, E, and Y. The second of the two manuscript hypotheses to H and TH omits the gods in H but mentions their more prominent role in TH.

michigan.apis.3161.s: Astronomical table for the calculation of the longitudes of the planet Mars, based on a division of the ecliptic into six zones coinciding with consecutive pairs of zodiacal signs, as in the Babylonian System A scheme for computing the phases of Mars; to each zone coresponds one table, in which a specific constant is multiplied by 1/3, 2/3, 1 ... 30 (right number in each column; the left number is the result of the multiplication). However, these constants are not those from the Babylonian theory, but have been modified to bring the Babylonian arithmetical scheme into agreement with a Greek geographical model of Mars's motion, with the result that the papyrus predicts very inaccurate longitudes

michigan.apis.3232.s: Will, in the form of a contract by which Psyphis alias Harpochration, son of Serapion alias Marepkemis, and his wife Tetosiris alias Dionysia, daughter of Maron alias Marepsemis, divide their property among their sons, daughters and grandsons; these take immediate possession of the property, and, in return, they are required to provide their parents with wheat, oil and money for clothing and expenses. (See also P.Mich. V, 238, l. 151, where this contract is recorded)

michigan.apis.3240.s: The content of this letter from Nilos to his brother Nemesion is somewhat unclear. First Nilos expresses his joy upon hearing that his brother had been released. The circumstances of this alone are unclear. Nilos also asks the brother to monitor a woman living in the house of a certain Kallinikos. It is not clear why he is supposed to; the text might imply that this action of Nemesion might free the woman from extortion; again the circumstances are very unclear. The verso contains the address.

michigan.apis.3241.t: Receipt (Certificate) for work performed for the penthemeral dyke corvȨe
michigan.apis.3241.s: Receipt (Certificate) for work performed on the embankments by Ptollis, son of Pamenes

michigan.apis.3242.s: Private letter in which Zoilos gives his sister Philoumene some advice concerning various matters.

michigan.apis.3243.s: This papyrus preserves the beginning of a petition to the strategos Agathos Daimon. In the text that survives the petitioner does not reach the substance of his complaint. After mentioning the dowry brought to him by his former wife, he begins a statement about the offspring of the marriage. Conceivably he then drew attention to some difficulty connected with the disposition of the dowry among the children, if indeed there were more than one.
michigan.apis.3243.luogo: Oxyrhynchos, Oxyrhynchite nome, Middle Egypt, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.3244.s: The text is an oath submitted to Hierax, royal secretary and acting strategos of the Oxyrhynchite nome, by two men from Sephtha in the lower toparchy. They were nominated to a liturgical office by the village secretary of Sephtha and they now present the usual oath. They are to set up a reception center for the idiotikoi onoi. The liturgy is here attested for the first time.
michigan.apis.3244.luogo: Oxyrhynchite nome, Middle Egypt, province of Egypt
k: Sephtha, village in the lower toparchy.

michigan.apis.3249.t: copy of a deed of sale
michigan.apis.3249.s: This papyrus contains the copy of a deed of sale. The buyer, . . .noitarion alias Thermouthion, has submitted to the archidicastes, Diodotos, a copy of the deed of sale of twenty-eight and a half arouras of land, including vineyards, plus a half-share of a water-wheel, which she purchased from Theogenes for 17,100 drachmas. The archidicastes has, in turn, submitted copies of the original contractand her request for publication to the Libraries of Hadrian and of the Nanaion; he has also returned to her a copy of the document as published, with his approval appended. She then sent a copy to the strategos with a request that he serve it on Theogenes. The text which we have is the copy which Theogenes received, since it bears his and a clerk's subscriptions acknowledging the serving of the document.

michigan.apis.3252.s: The document's chief interest resides in its mention of a Ceasarium built at Antinoopolis. This information, while hardly surprising, is new. In Egypt Caesarea are recorded also at Alexandria, Arsinoe, Hermopolis and Oxyrhynchos. The petitioners ask for their salry for the month Phamenoth.

michigan.apis.3253.t: A petition to strategos of Oasis Minor (?)
michigan.apis.3253.s: A petition to the strategos asking that the person against whom the complaint is lodged be obliged to post security till the matter is settled at the forthcoming visit of the Prefect and the Idiologos. The lost of the text at the right hand side leaves us in the dark on the nature and details of the dispute.
michigan.apis.3253.luogo: Small Oasis, Middle Egypt, province of Egypt

michigan.apis.3433.t: List of villages in the Themistou meris
michigan.apis.3433.s: A list of villages with amounts of grain credited to each by certain individuals who were undoubtedly sitologoi. Of the 12 villages named, 3 of them whose location has not been previously known with any exactness, have marginal notes describing them as adjacent to specific villages whose locations are vely well known to us due to the excavations of Grenfell and Hunt. These are: Ptolemais, Ptolemais Drymou and Alexandrou Nesos, which are said to be adjacent to Euemeria, Dionysias and Theadelphia respectively.
